origin.audio: The expansion of community gardens has led to a reduction in food costs for many families. One researcher, however, warns that the allocation of scarce land could divide neighbourhoods, unless councils explain their rules openly. In plain English: more people are growing their own food, and they save money, but there is not enough land for everybody, so somebody has to decide who gets it, and people must be able to trust that decision.

prompt.es: Resume el artículo en un texto nominal de unas 160 palabras.

answer.text: The fast expansion of community gardens in European cities has led to a marked reduction in stress and in food costs for many families, according to a growing body of evidence. Researchers who followed four hundred gardeners for two years also found that participation brings neighbours together and encourages them to share tools, seeds and advice. However, this expansion is limited by a shortage of vacant land, and councils disagree about the allocation of plots: some would give priority to schools, others to older residents, and a few to whoever has waited longest. One researcher warns that the lack of a fair system could turn a popular project into a source of anger. A key finding of the study is that gardens work well when residents help to make the rules. The next step, therefore, is a transparent system for the allocation of land that every neighbour can understand and trust. In short, the gardens offer clear social and health benefits, but only a fair allocation of land will allow them to keep growing.
accepted: The fast expansion of community gardens in European cities has led to a marked reduction in stress and in food costs for many families, according to a growing body of evidence. Researchers who followed four hundred gardeners for two years also found that participation brings neighbours together and encourages them to share tools, seeds and advice. However, this expansion is limited by a shortage of vacant land, and councils disagree about the allocation of plots: some would give priority to schools, others to older residents, and a few to whoever has waited longest. One researcher warns that the lack of a fair system could turn a popular project into a source of anger. A key finding of the study is that gardens work well when residents help to make the rules. The next step, therefore, is a transparent system for the allocation of land that every neighbour can understand and trust. In short, the gardens offer clear social and health benefits, but only a fair allocation of land will allow them to keep growing.

Community gardens are growing quickly in European cities, and researchers who followed four hundred gardeners report a reduction in stress and lower spending on food. Participation also brings neighbours together, since they share tools, seeds and advice. The expansion, however, is limited: vacant land is scarce, and councils cannot agree on the allocation of plots, because some prefer schools, others older residents and a few those who have waited longest. One researcher warns that the lack of a fair system could produce anger instead of cooperation. According to the study, gardens work well when residents help to make the rules, so the next step is a transparent system that everybody can understand and trust. A growing body of evidence suggests that the benefits of these gardens go well beyond fresh food.

feedback.es: Un buen resumen nominal nombra la expansión, el efecto (una reducción), la participación, el límite (falta de terreno y reparto) y el siguiente paso.

origin.text: Community gardens are spreading fast through European cities. In many capitals, empty corners that used to be ignored by everybody are now full of vegetables and flowers. In the last ten years, thousands of neighbours have started to grow vegetables together on small plots of public land, and a growing body of evidence suggests that the benefits go well beyond fresh food. Researchers who followed four hundred gardeners for two years report a marked reduction in stress, and many families say that they now spend less money on food. One gardener, a retired teacher, says that she knows more neighbours now than she did in thirty years in the same street. Participation has also brought people together: in several districts, neighbours who had never spoken now share tools, seeds and advice. Local newspapers have run many stories about the gardens, and several mayors have visited them. However, the expansion has a clear limit. Vacant land is scarce, and councils disagree about the allocation of the plots. In some districts a neighbour may wait three years for a plot. Some want to give them first to schools, others to older residents, and a few argue that the places should go to whoever has waited longest. One researcher warns that the lack of a fair system could turn a popular project into a source of anger. A key finding of the study is that gardens work well when residents help to make the rules. The next step, she says, is a transparent system that every neighbour can understand and trust.
